Aromatic L-Amino Acid Decarboxylase (AADC, DDC): Technical Overview Gene and Protein Nomenclature: The human AADC enzyme is encoded by the DDC gene (official symbol DDC, chromosomal region 7p12.2–p12.1) . The official gene name is dopa decarboxylase, and the protein is formally aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (AADC), a member of the lyase family (EC 4.1.1.28) . Synonyms include L‑dopa decarboxylase, tryptophan decarboxylase, and 5‑hydroxytryptophan decarboxylase . AADC is a homodimeric enzyme requiring pyridoxal-5′-phosphate (PLP) and mediates the final step in monoamine neurotransmitter synthesis. -Enzymatic Function and Mechanism: AADC catalyzes irreversible α‑decarboxylation of aromatic L-amino acids. In particular, it converts L‑3,4‑dihydroxyphenylalanine (L‑DOPA) to dopamine and L‑5‑hydroxytryptophan (5‑HTP) to serotonin . (It also decarboxylates L‑tryptophan to tryptamine and L‑phenylalanine to phenethylamine, producing trace amines.) The enzyme’s reaction mechanism is the canonical PLP-dependent decarboxylase mechanism: PLP is bound as an internal Schiff base to Lys303 in each monomer . When substrate (e.g. L‑DOPA) enters the active site, its amino group displaces Lys303 and forms an external Schiff base with PLP . This properly orients the substrate’s carboxylate for decarboxylation, yielding a quinonoid intermediate. Subsequent protonation of this intermediate produces the Schiff base of PLP with the decarboxylated amine (e.g. dopamine) . Finally, Lys303 attacks the Schiff base, regenerating the internal aldimine and releasing the free product (CO₂ is released in the decarboxylation step). These steps have been confirmed by structural studies of human AADC in various states.
11:20 PM
Substrates and Products (IUPAC Names & Structures): AADC’s primary substrates and products are aromatic amino acids and amines. Key examples include: • L-3,4-Dihydroxyphenylalanine (L-DOPA): IUPAC: (2S)-2-amino-3-(3,4-dihydroxyphenyl)propanoic acid . Formula: C₉H₁₁NO₄ . (C₉H₁₁NO₄, M_w ≈197.19). AADC removes CO₂ from L-DOPA to form dopamine. • Dopamine (DA): IUPAC: 4-(2-Aminoethyl)benzene-1,2-diol . Formula: C₈H₁₁NO₂ . Dopamine is the catecholamine product from L-DOPA decarboxylation (and precursor to norepinephrine/epinephrine). • L-5-Hydroxytryptophan (5-HTP): IUPAC: 2-amino-3-(5-hydroxy-1H-indol-3-yl)propanoic acid . Formula: C₁₁H₁₂N₂O₃ . AADC decarboxylates 5-HTP to produce serotonin. • Serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine, 5-HT): Preferred IUPAC: 3-(2-aminoethyl)-1H-indol-5-ol (other name 5-hydroxytryptamine ). Formula: C₁₀H₁₂N₂O . Serotonin is the indoleamine product of 5-HTP decarboxylation. (Other AADC substrates include L-tryptophan → tryptamine, and L-phenylalanine → phenethylamine; their structures are similarly aromatic L-amino acids. Histidine decarboxylation to histamine is not catalyzed by AADC but by histidine decarboxylase.)
11:21 PM
Neurotransmitter Biosynthesis Pathways: AADC-mediated decarboxylation is the final step in both catecholamine and indolamine biosynthesis. In neurons: • Dopamine pathway: Tyrosine → (tyrosine hydroxylase) → L-DOPA → (AADC) → dopamine . Dopamine can then be hydroxylated to norepinephrine and methylated to epinephrine. In Parkinson’s disease therapy, peripheral AADC is blocked to allow more L-DOPA to reach the brain . • Serotonin pathway: Tryptophan → (tryptophan hydroxylase) → 5-HTP → (AADC) → serotonin . Serotonin can be further converted to melatonin in the pineal gland. AADC is not normally rate-limiting, but in L-DOPA-treated PD patients it becomes the bottleneck for dopamine production . Note that histamine synthesis (histidine → histamine) uses a different enzyme (HDC) and is independent of AADC. Role in Model Organisms: The function of AADC is highly conserved. In Drosophila, the Ddc gene encodes AADC and its mutations drastically reduce dopamine and serotonin synthesis , impairing learning and behavior. In Caenorhabditis elegans, the bas-1 gene encodes an AADC required for converting 5-HTP to serotonin (bas-1 mutants cannot produce serotonin from 5-HTP). In zebrafish (Danio rerio), a single ddc homolog (AADC) shares ~88% identity with human AADC . Zebrafish ddc is expressed in catecholaminergic brain regions (locus coeruleus, raphe nuclei, etc.) . Knockdown or inhibition of zebrafish ddc causes developmental and motor defects reminiscent of human AADC deficiency , validating zebrafish as a model for this disorder. In mice, complete Ddc knockout is embryonically lethal (no viable pups) due to profound monoamine deficit (in practice, only hypomorphic or conditional alleles exist in the literature). Allosteric Regulation, Inhibitors, and Activators: AADC activity depends on its PLP cofactor (pyridoxal phosphate, vitamin B₆) ultimately.
11:21 PM
PLP binds to Lys303 to form the Schiff base; without PLP (e.g. in B₆ deficiency), serotonin synthesis is especially impaired. Phosphorylation can modulate AADC activity: for example, PKA and PKG can phosphorylate the enzyme and increase its activity (studies by Duchemin et al.). No small-molecule allosteric activators are in clinical use, but the cofactor PLP itself is essential (high-dose pyridoxine can sometimes boost residual AADC activity in partial deficiency). Clinically important inhibitors of AADC are used in Parkinson’s therapy: • Carbidopa: An irreversible peripheral AADC inhibitor that does not cross the blood–brain barrier . When given with L-DOPA, carbidopa prevents L-DOPA’s peripheral decarboxylation, increasing central dopamine levels (and reducing peripheral side effects). • Benserazide: Similar to carbidopa, benserazide is a peripherally acting AADC inhibitor unable to cross into the brain . It is used with L-DOPA in many countries (e.g. as co-careldopa). • Alpha-methyldopa: (Indirect) is taken up by AADC and converted to alpha-methyldopamine; less potent than above for inhibition. Other compounds (e.g. quinones, EGCG) have been studied as AADC inhibitors, but carbidopa/benserazide are the primary clinical ones.
11:22 PM
Downstream Metabolic and Neurological Effects: Inhibition or loss of AADC has major effects on neurotransmitter levels. In AADC deficiency (bi-allelic DDC mutations), patients have almost no dopamine or serotonin (nor norepinephrine/epinephrine) and accumulate precursors (e.g. 3-O-methyldopa, 5-HTP) . Clinically, AADC-deficient infants present with oculogyric crises, dystonia, hypotonia, autonomic dysfunction and developmental delay . These symptoms reflect combined catecholamine and serotonin deficiency: dopamine deficit impairs movement and cognition, norepinephrine/epinephrine deficit affects attention and autonomic tone, and serotonin deficit affects mood, sleep, and endocrine regulation . In Parkinson’s disease (PD), loss of dopaminergic neurons leads to dopamine deficiency. AADC remains intact in surviving neurons, so exogenous L-DOPA can be used to restore dopamine. The addition of carbidopa/benserazide enhances L-DOPA’s central efficacy . DDC polymorphisms can modify L-DOPA response in PD: for example, a common variant (Gly102Ser) alters enzyme kinetics and can influence treatment response. However, DDC gene is not a major PD risk gene.
11:22 PM
Structural and Biochemical Insights: AADC has been crystallized in multiple states. Early structures (PDB 1JS3, 3RBL, 8OR9) revealed a pyridoxal-phosphate bound enzyme and its conformational changes. These X-ray structures show AADC as a PLP-dependent homodimer, with each active site at the dimer interface. Lys303 binds PLP; key catalytic residues (e.g. Tyr271, His192 in human) position substrate for decarboxylation. Crystal structures with inhibitors (e.g. carbidopa) illuminate binding interactions. Mutagenesis studies confirm Lys303 is essential for activity, and alterations of nearby residues (Thr82, Ser149, etc.) affect substrate binding and catalysis . Kinetic analyses in the literature report typical Km values in the low micromolar range for L-DOPA and 5-HTP, and pH optima near physiological pH (optimum around pH 6.7 for L-DOPA, ~7.2 for 5-HTP). Spectroscopic and biochemical assays show that AADC forms a quinonoid intermediate detectable at ~500 nm during catalysis. PLP binding induces the characteristic absorbance at 412 nm (Schiff base). Some studies suggest subtle isoforms or microenvironments distinguish dopamine vs. serotonin decarboxylation (consistent with the differing pH optima observed).
11:22 PM
Genetic Variants and Disease Associations: Pathogenic DDC variants cause autosomal recessive AADC deficiency (OMIM #608643) . Over 30 disease-causing mutations have been reported. Examples include: c.304G>A (p.Gly102Ser), a catalytically impaired variant associated with a “levodopa-responsive” phenotype ; c.714+4A>T, a common splice-site founder variant in East Asian populations; and missense variants like p.Arg347Gln or p.Arg412Trp . These typically reduce enzyme activity to a few percent of normal. Clinical severity correlates with residual activity. The GeneReviews summary lists many such variants . DDC polymorphisms have also been studied in Parkinson’s disease. For example, the promoter SNP rs921451 was reported to influence motor response to L-DOPA (though it does not cause PD itself). Thus, while DDC mutations underlie a rare pediatric deficiency syndrome, common variants may modulate drug response in Parkinsonism.
11:22 PM
Transporters and Cofactor Dependence: After synthesis, monoamines are handled by specific transporters. Dopamine released into the synaptic cleft is rapidly cleared by the dopamine transporter (DAT; SLC6A3) back into presynaptic neurons . Serotonin is similarly cleared by the serotonin transporter (SERT). For storage, vesicular monoamine transporter 2 (VMAT2; SLC18A2) sequesters dopamine, serotonin, and other monoamines into synaptic vesicles . Effective neurotransmission thus requires intact AADC together with DAT and VMAT2 for recycling and release. AADC’s enzymatic activity absolutely requires its cofactor PLP (the active form of vitamin B₆) . PLP is covalently attached to Lys303, and it shuttles between internal and external aldimine forms during catalysis . Vitamin B₆ deficiency or genetic defects in B₆ metabolism can thus secondarily impair AADC function (reducing dopamine/serotonin levels). In AADC-deficient patients, pyridoxine (B₆) supplementation is often tried as a partial treatment.
11:24 PM
Enzyme Profiles: Oxidoreductases / 3-HAO (HAAO – 3-Hydroxyanthranilate 3,4-Dioxygenase) 3-HAO, encoded by HAAO, is a non-heme iron dioxygenase that catalyzes the oxidative ring cleavage of 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid into 2-amino-3-carboxymuconate semialdehyde, which spontaneously cyclizes to quinolinic acid . This reaction is the penultimate step in the kynurenine (tryptophan catabolism) pathway, linking tryptophan degradation to de novo NAD⁺ synthesis . HAAO is expressed in mammals (high in liver and kidney) and many bacteria, controlling quinolinic acid (QUIN) levels. QUIN is an excitotoxic NMDA-receptor agonist; HAAO thus influences neurotoxic QUIN accumulation. Defects or altered regulation of HAAO have been implicated in neurological and inflammatory diseases associated with elevated QUIN . Notably, pharmacological HAAO inhibitors have been explored: raising 3-hydroxyanthranilate levels reduces atherosclerosis in mice by downregulating SREBP2 and lowering lipid accumulation . No common loss-of-function variants are known in humans, but targeted inhibitors (e.g. NCR-631) are under investigation as metabolic regulators.
11:25 PM
L-Amino Acid Oxidase (LAAO) is a flavoprotein oxidase that catalyzes the oxidative deamination of L-amino acids to α-keto acids, producing ammonia and hydrogen peroxide as byproducts. Widely distributed in organisms including bacteria, fungi, snakes, and mammals, LAAOs have been extensively studied for their biochemical versatility and physiological roles. In snake venoms, LAAOs contribute to antimicrobial, apoptotic, and hemorrhagic activities, often enhancing toxicity through the generation of hydrogen peroxide. In microbial systems such as Rhizobium etli and Pseudomonas species, LAAOs are implicated in nitrogen metabolism and secondary metabolite biosynthesis. Structurally, LAAOs are characterized by a conserved FAD-binding domain, essential for redox activity, and a substrate-binding site tailored to L-amino acid specificity. Recent research has explored LAAOs in the context of biotechnological and therapeutic applications. For instance, bacterial and fungal LAAOs are under investigation for their use in biosensors, cancer therapy (due to their selective cytotoxicity), and antimicrobial drug development. Moreover, their involvement in interspecies signaling and innate immunity positions LAAOs as key targets in host-pathogen interaction studies. Advanced structural analyses, including X-ray crystallography and molecular dynamics simulations, have revealed dynamic features of substrate channeling and active site conformational changes, offering insight into engineering LAAOs with altered specificity or enhanced activity. As such, LAAOs serve as a compelling model for redox biochemistry and a promising scaffold for novel biomedical strategies.
11:26 PM
ACMSD (Aminocarboxymuconate Semialdehyde Decarboxylase) ACMSD diverts tryptophan catabolism away from quinolinic acid/NAD⁺ synthesis. It catalyzes the decarboxylation of α-amino-β-carboxymuconate-ε-semialdehyde (ACMS) into 2-aminomuconate semialdehyde . By this reaction, ACMSD prevents accumulation of quinolinic acid (a neurotoxin) and yields metabolites leading to picolinic acid . ACMSD (cytosolic enzyme) is highly expressed in kidney and liver (humans and rodents) . Genetic models show that overexpression of ACMSD in mice creates niacin (vitamin B3) dependency by shunting away NAD⁺ synthesis . Human ACMSD mutations cause hyperkynureninemia with neurological features (epilepsy, movement disorders) . ACMSD variants have been linked to suicide risk and Parkinsonism. Inhibitors of ACMSD are being explored to increase 3-hydroxyanthranilate levels and counteract high cholesterol: one study showed ACMSD inhibition lowers hepatic SREBP-2 and plasma lipids . ACMSD thus plays a critical role in balancing NAD⁺ precursor production vs. neurotoxic byproducts.
11:27 PM
ACS (Acetate/Acyl-CoA Synthetases) “ACS” enzymes activate acetate (and other short-chain acids) by forming acyl-CoA derivatives. In humans, mitochondrial ACSS1 and cytosolic ACSS2 are acetyl-CoA synthetases: they catalyze acetate + CoA + ATP → acetyl-CoA + AMP + PPi . This provides acetyl-CoA for the TCA cycle, lipid synthesis and histone acetylation . ACSS2 (cytosolic) supplies acetyl-CoA for fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis and epigenetic modifications (nuclear acetylation). ACSS1 (mitochondrial) fuels energy production from acetate. In microbes (e.g. E. coli acs), ACS is essential for growth on acetate. Humans also have long-chain acyl-CoA synthetase (ACSL) enzymes for lipid metabolism. No common loss-of-function ACS1/2 mutations are known, but ACSS2 is often upregulated in cancers under metabolic stress . ACSS enzymes are all ATP-dependent ligases and can be inhibited by analogs of CoA or AMP. For example, ACSS2 inhibitors are investigated for cancer therapy (starving tumor cells of acetyl-CoA) . ADH (Alcohol Dehydrogenase) ADH refers to the NAD⁺-dependent alcohol dehydrogenase family that oxidize alcohols to aldehydes. The human ADH family has multiple genes (7 total): class I (ADH1A, B, C) in liver performs ethanol → acetaldehyde conversion, and also oxidizes retinol to retinal . Other classes (II-V) have broader substrate specificity. ADHs are zinc-containing enzymes. In yeast and plants, ADH is important for fermentation.
11:27 PM
Polymorphisms (e.g. ADH1B2) alter enzyme activity: the fast-acting ADH1B2 allele leads to rapid acetaldehyde accumulation and flushing. ADH plays key roles in alcohol metabolism; its acetaldehyde product is toxic and then cleared by ALDH. Clinically, ADH variants affect alcoholism risk. ADH deficiency is lethal in most mammals. ADH is allosterically regulated by substrate levels. Research on ADH includes its roles in retinoid metabolism and drug biotransformation. For example, ADH1A transcription is induced by retinoic acid, linking vitamin A and ethanol metabolism.
11:28 PM
ALDH (Aldehyde Dehydrogenases) The human ALDH superfamily (~19 isoenzymes) oxidizes aldehydes to acids using NAD(P)⁺ . Key isoforms include mitochondrial ALDH2 (acetaldehyde → acetate) and cytosolic ALDH1A1 (retinal → retinoic acid). ALDH2 is abundant in liver, heart and muscle . ALDHs serve in detoxification (e.g. lipid peroxidation products) and biosynthesis (formic acid, GABA). The classic example is ethanol metabolism: ADH generates acetaldehyde, then ALDH2 clears it. The ALDH2*2 variant (common in East Asians) greatly reduces activity, causing flushing and higher risk for cancer . Inhibitors like disulfiram irreversibly inhibit ALDH (mainly ALDH2), causing toxic acetaldehyde accumulation . ALDHs also include glutamate dehydrogenase-like (ALDH8) and retinal dehydrogenases. ALDH dysfunction is implicated in alcohol intolerance, cancer, and neurodegeneration. Overall, NAD(P)-dependent ALDHs are central to aldehyde clearance and cofactor regeneration .
11:28 PM
ALT (Alanine Aminotransferase, GPT) ALT refers to alanine transaminase (cytosolic ALT1/GPT), with a mitochondrial isoform (ALT2, GPT2). These PLP-dependent enzymes catalyze L-alanine + α-ketoglutarate ⇌ pyruvate + L-glutamate , linking amino acid and carbohydrate metabolism. ALT1 (GPT) is enriched in liver, reflecting its role in gluconeogenesis via the Cahill (alanine) cycle. ALT2 (mitochondrial) also supports this shuttle. Elevated serum ALT is a clinical marker of hepatocellular injury . Genetic deficiencies are extremely rare, but GPT2 mutations cause developmental encephalopathy . ALT expression is transcriptionally regulated by nutrient status and hormones (e.g. glucocorticoids). AST (Aspartate Aminotransferase, GOT) AST includes a cytosolic isozyme (GOT1) and a mitochondrial isozyme (GOT2). Both use PLP to catalyze L-aspartate + α-ketoglutarate ⇌ oxaloacetate + L-glutamate . AST enzymes shuttle amino groups between TCA intermediates and amino acids, participating in the malate–aspartate shuttle and the urea cycle . GOT1 (cytosol) and GOT2 (mitochondria) are abundant in heart, liver, and muscle. Clinically, AST levels rise with tissue injury (liver, myocardium). GOT2 is essential for the mitochondrial shuttle; GOT1 provides cytosolic balance. Loss of both isoforms is lethal in mice. AST activity is regulated by substrate availability and by ALT interplay, preserving NAD⁺/NADH balance between compartments.
11:29 PM
AMPK (AMP-Activated Protein Kinase) AMPK is a cellular energy sensor, not strictly an oxidoreductase, but included for its metabolic role. It is a heterotrimeric Ser/Thr kinase (α catalytic, β regulatory, γ nucleotide-binding subunits) activated by increases in AMP/ADP (low energy) . Once activated (by AMP-binding and phosphorylation by LKB1/CaMKK2), AMPK phosphorylates targets to inhibit anabolic pathways and activate catabolic pathways, thus restoring energy balance . This includes inactivation of acetyl-CoA carboxylase (fatty acid synthesis), inhibition of mTORC1, and stimulation of glucose uptake and fatty acid oxidation. The genes are PRKAA1/2 (α1/α2), PRKAB1/2 (β1/β2), PRKAG1/2/3 (γ1/2/3). Tissue-specific expression and isoform composition vary (e.g. PRKAG3 in muscle). Dysregulated AMPK is implicated in metabolic disease and cancer; its activation is a mechanism of drugs like metformin. No direct metabolites as substrates are known; instead, AMPK is regulated by adenylates and post-translational modifications. CAT (Catalase) Catalase, encoded by CAT, is a heme enzyme in peroxisomes that decomposes hydrogen peroxide: 2 H₂O₂ → 2 H₂O + O₂ . By rapidly converting toxic H₂O₂ into water and oxygen , catalase protects cells from oxidative damage. It is one of the most abundant antioxidant enzymes in aerobic organisms (high in liver). Humans have a single catalase gene (with pseudogenes); catalase is a tetramer of ~60 kDa subunits each containing an Fe-heme. Genetic deficiency (acatalasemia) is rare but predisposes to oxidative stress; some polymorphisms reduce activity (linked to diabetes risk ). Catalase is distinct from glutathione peroxidase (Se-dependent) and glutathione reductase. It is regulated by substrate availability (high H₂O₂) and nitric oxide. No endogenous inhibitors are known, but 3-amino-1,2,4-triazole can irreversibly inhibit catalase.
11:29 PM
CBS (Cystathionine β-Synthase) CBS is a PLP-dependent enzyme that catalyzes the condensation of homocysteine with serine to form cystathionine (and subsequently cysteine) in the transsulfuration pathway . This is the first committed step linking methionine metabolism to cysteine and glutathione synthesis. CBS is a heme-containing homotetramer regulated by S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) – SAM binding activates CBS . Human CBS (gene CBS) is highly expressed in liver and brain. Mutations in CBS cause classical homocystinuria (accumulation of homocysteine), leading to vascular and neurological disease . Additionally, CBS generates H₂S gas as a byproduct, playing roles in cellular signaling. No major isoforms are reported (except minor transcripts). Pharmacologically, CBS inhibitors are studied to modulate H₂S in disease, while SAM analogs can regulate CBS activity. COMT (Catechol-O-Methyltransferase) COMT (gene COMT) is a magnesium-dependent methyltransferase that transfers a methyl group from SAM to catechols. It catalyzes the inactivation of catechol neurotransmitters and hormones: for example, dopamine → 3-methoxytyramine and norepinephrine → normetanephrine . Human COMT exists in two forms from a single gene: a soluble cytosolic form (S-COMT) and a membrane-bound form (MB-COMT) differing by an N-terminal extension. COMT is expressed in liver, kidney, brain, and placenta. A common Val158Met polymorphism affects enzyme stability: the Met variant has lower activity and is linked to differences in executive function and psychiatric disorders. COMT inhibitors (tolcapone, entacapone) are clinically used with L-DOPA to prevent peripheral dopamine methylation in Parkinson’s disease . COMT also methylates catechol estrogens; its regulation and polymorphisms have been studied in relation to cancer risk.
11:29 PM
G6PDH (Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase) G6PDH, encoded by G6PD on the X chromosome, catalyzes the rate-limiting first step of the pentose phosphate pathway: G6P + NADP⁺ → 6-phosphoglucono-δ-lactone + NADPH. G6PDH is a cytosolic enzyme whose main function is to generate NADPH for reductive biosynthesis and for maintaining glutathione in its reduced form . It is abundantly expressed in red blood cells, phagocytes, and liver. Human G6PD is highly polymorphic: deficiency variants (e.g. Mediterranean, African A-) reduce enzyme activity, leading to vulnerability to hemolytic anemia under oxidative stress. G6PDH regulation is primarily via NADP⁺ availability. The enzyme is essential for cell survival under oxidative conditions. Recent studies implicate G6PDH in cancer and metabolic diseases, as it provides NADPH for anabolic growth. GAPDH (Glyceraldehyde-3-Phosphate Dehydrogenase) GAPDH is a glycolytic enzyme (gene GAPDH) that catalyzes glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate + NAD⁺ + Pi ⇌ 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate + NADH + H⁺ . This step yields NADH and a high-energy acyl phosphate in glycolysis. GAPDH is ubiquitously expressed and generally constitutive (“housekeeping”), but has diverse “moonlighting” roles in transcription regulation, apoptosis, and vesicular transport.
11:30 PM
GAPDH is regulated by oxidative modifications (nitrosylation, acetylation) that can inhibit its activity. Clinically, GAPDH overexpression is noted in many cancers (supporting glycolysis). Despite its central role, genetic disruption of GAPDH is lethal. In research, GAPDH expression is commonly used as a control gene. No physiological isoforms are reported in humans (multiple pseudogenes exist). GPX (Glutathione Peroxidase) The GPX family includes several selenoenzymes that reduce peroxides using glutathione. GPX1 (cytosolic, ubiquitous) catalyzes 2 GSH + H₂O₂ → GSSG + 2 H₂O , protecting cells from oxidative damage. Other isoforms (GPX2–GPX4) have distinct substrate preferences and tissue distributions. All are homotetramers (except GPX4 is monomeric) with selenocysteine at the active site . GPX enzymes are induced by oxidative stress via Nrf2 signaling. GPX1 variants (e.g. a polyalanine repeat) are associated with cancer risk . Glutathione peroxidases are kept active by glutathione reductase (see GR below) and require adequate selenium in the diet. Inhibition of GPX (e.g. by mercuric compounds) leads to oxidative injury.
11:30 PM
GR (Glutathione Reductase) GR, encoded by GSR, is a flavoprotein homodimer that maintains the cellular glutathione pool . It uses NADPH to reduce oxidized glutathione (GSSG) back to 2 GSH: GSSG + NADPH + H⁺ → 2 GSH + NADP⁺ . By regenerating GSH, GR is central to antioxidant defense in virtually all tissues. GR is localized in the cytosol and mitochondria. Rare human GR deficiencies (mutations in GSR) cause hemolytic anemia under oxidative stress. GR activity is regulated by NADPH availability (linked to G6PDH activity). The enzyme is also implicated in redox-related signaling. Inhibitors of GR (e.g. BCNU/carmustine) deplete GSH and sensitize cells to oxidative damage; conversely, GR overexpression can confer chemoresistance.
11:31 PM
IDO1 (Indoleamine 2,3-Dioxygenase 1) IDO1 is a heme-containing dioxygenase that catalyzes the first, rate-limiting step of the kynurenine pathway in extrahepatic tissues. It oxidizes L-tryptophan (and several analogs) to N-formylkynurenine , using O₂ and yielding H₂O in the process. IDO1 is induced by inflammatory cytokines (especially IFN-γ) in dendritic cells, macrophages, and tumors. The depletion of local tryptophan and production of kynurenine metabolites by IDO1 suppresses T-cell proliferation, contributing to immunoregulation and tolerance . Clinically, IDO1 expression is associated with tumor immune evasion and chronic inflammation. Small-molecule IDO1 inhibitors have been developed (e.g. epacadostat) for cancer therapy, though with mixed results. IDO1’s activity is regulated at transcriptional (cytokines) and post-translational levels, and it is inhibited by nitric oxide and some metabolites.
11:31 PM
TDO2 (Tryptophan 2,3-Dioxygenase) TDO2 (gene TDO2) is a heme enzyme primarily expressed in the liver that catalyzes the same reaction as IDO1: the oxidation of L-tryptophan to N-formylkynurenine, initiating the kynurenine pathway . Unlike IDO1, TDO2 expression is relatively constant but upregulated by glucocorticoids and high tryptophan levels. TDO2 supplies kynurenine for NAD⁺ biosynthesis and regulates systemic tryptophan levels. High TDO2 activity (e.g. in tumors) can also contribute to immune suppression via kynurenine production . Rare polymorphisms in TDO2 have been linked to neurodevelopmental traits (e.g. autism susceptibility ). Inhibitors of TDO2 (e.g. LM10) are being explored for cancer immunotherapy. KAT (Kynurenine Aminotransferases) Kynurenine aminotransferases (KATs) are PLP-dependent enzymes that transaminate L-kynurenine to kynurenic acid (KYNA), a neuroactive metabolite . Mammals have four KAT isoenzymes (KAT I–IV) with differing tissue distributions. For example, KAT II (encoded by AADAT) predominates in brain for producing KYNA, an antagonist of NMDA and α7-nicotinic receptors . The KATs also act on 3-hydroxykynurenine to form 3-hydroxykynurenic acid. By controlling the balance between neuroprotective KYNA and neurotoxic quinolinic acid, KATs influence neuronal excitotoxicity. Dysregulation of KYNA levels (via altered KAT activity) has been implicated in schizophrenia and neurodegeneration . Specific KAT inhibitors and activators are under study for neurological diseases.
11:31 PM
KMO (Kynurenine 3-Monooxygenase) KMO, located on the outer mitochondrial membrane, hydroxylates L-kynurenine to 3-hydroxykynurenine . This NADPH-dependent enzyme drives tryptophan metabolites toward the production of quinolinic acid (via 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid). KMO is highly expressed in liver, kidney, and microglia. By diverting kynurenine away from KYNA, KMO influences neurotoxic metabolite levels. Inhibiting KMO is a major research focus for neuroprotection: KMO blockade raises KYNA and lowers 3-HK/quinolinate, showing benefit in models of Huntington’s and neuroinflammation . KMO variants have been associated with psychiatric disorders, and small-molecule KMO inhibitors (e.g. Ro 61-8048) are being evaluated experimentally. KYNU (Kynureninase) Kynureninase is a PLP-dependent enzyme that cleaves L-kynurenine and L-3-hydroxykynurenine into anthranilic acid and 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid, respectively . It thus operates downstream in the kynurenine pathway, contributing to NAD⁺ biosynthesis from tryptophan. Human KYNU (encoded by KYNU) is expressed in liver, kidney, and brain. Mutations in KYNU cause a rare form of pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy due to accumulation of upstream metabolites. Regulation of KYNU is less studied, but it likely depends on cofactor (PLP) availability and substrate levels. The enzyme has multiple transcript variants, although all produce active enzyme . Inhibitors of kynureninase are being explored to modulate neuroactive metabolite levels.
11:32 PM
LDH (Lactate Dehydrogenase) Lactate dehydrogenases (LDH) are NAD(H)-dependent enzymes catalyzing L-lactate + NAD⁺ ↔ pyruvate + NADH + H⁺ . In humans, LDH exists as tetramers of two subunit types: LDHA (“muscle” A-subunit) and LDHB (“heart” B-subunit). Isozyme composition (e.g. LDH5=A₄, LDH1=B₄) varies by tissue and dictates kinetic properties. During anaerobic glycolysis, LDH regenerates NAD⁺ by reducing pyruvate to lactate. LDH is also involved in gluconeogenesis (in reverse). Clinically, serum LDH levels (and isoenzyme ratios) rise in tissue damage (heart attack, hemolysis, cancer). In cancer, LDH-A (PKM2 upstream, LDHA downstream) is often upregulated (Warburg effect). LDH activity is allosterically inhibited by high NADH or pyruvate, and by the drug gossypol. No serious LDH genetic diseases are known, as multiple isoenzymes compensate.
11:32 PM
MAO (Monoamine Oxidases A and B) MAO-A and MAO-B are FAD-dependent enzymes in the mitochondrial outer membrane that catalyze oxidative deamination of biogenic amines. They convert amines (e.g. dopamine, serotonin, tyramine) into the corresponding aldehydes, releasing NH₃ and H₂O₂. MAO-A preferentially degrades serotonin, norepinephrine and dopamine, while MAO-B prefers phenethylamine and benzylamine (both metabolize dopamine) . Both isoforms require oxygen and produce H₂O₂ as byproduct. MAO-A (gene MAOA) is widely expressed in neurons and gut, MAO-B (MAOB) in astrocytes and platelets. Inhibitors of MAO-A (e.g. clorgyline) and MAO-B (e.g. selegiline) are used clinically to treat depression and Parkinson’s disease by elevating neurotransmitter levels. MAO activity affects mood and cardiovascular regulation; rare MAO-A deficiency causes Brunner syndrome (behavioral abnormalities). Regulation of MAO involves gene promoter polymorphisms and factors like cortisol.
11:33 PM
MDH (Malate Dehydrogenase) MDH exists as two isoenzymes: mitochondrial MDH2 and cytosolic MDH1. Both catalyze L-malate + NAD⁺ ↔ oxaloacetate + NADH + H⁺, a reversible step in the TCA cycle and gluconeogenesis . MDH2 (mitochondrial) participates in the TCA cycle and the malate–aspartate shuttle; MDH1 (cytosolic) functions in gluconeogenesis and shuttling reducing equivalents. Human MDH1 and MDH2 are encoded by separate genes and have distinct targeting signals. No major human MDH deficiencies are known; however, MDH1 overexpression or MDH2 mutations have been implicated in cancer and metabolic disease. MDH activity is regulated by NAD⁺/NADH ratio and by the malate concentration. ME1 (Malic Enzyme 1) ME1 is the cytosolic, NADP⁺-dependent malic enzyme . It catalyzes the reversible oxidative decarboxylation of malate to pyruvate, generating NADPH (malate + NADP⁺ → pyruvate + CO₂ + NADPH) . This links glycolysis, the TCA cycle, and lipid synthesis: ME1 provides NADPH for fatty acid synthesis and contributes pyruvate back into metabolism. ME1 expression is regulated by diet and hormones: it is induced by high carbohydrates and by thyroid hormones . In mice, ME1 deficiency causes altered lipid metabolism. In humans, ME1 is overexpressed in some cancers (supporting redox balance) . ME1 activity is inhibited by ATP and promoted by fructose 1,6-bisphosphate, coordinating with glycolytic flux.
11:33 PM
MTHFR (Methylenetetrahydrofolate Reductase) MTHFR is a flavoprotein that catalyzes 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate → 5-methyltetrahydrofolate . The latter is the methyl donor for remethylating homocysteine to methionine. MTHFR thus bridges folate and methionine cycles. It requires FAD as a cofactor and is inhibited by high S-adenosylmethionine (feedback). A common MTHFR polymorphism (C677T, Ala222Val) results in thermolabile enzyme with reduced activity, leading to mild hyperhomocysteinemia. MTHFR variants are associated with neural tube defect risk, cardiovascular disease, and certain cancers . MTHFR deficiency causes homocystinuria (neonatal homocystinuria with megaloblastic anemia). Current research explores interactions between folate levels, MTHFR genotype, and epigenetic methylation. NAMPT (Nicotinamide Phosphoribosyltransferase) NAMPT (also called visfatin/PBEF) catalyzes the rate-limiting step in the NAD⁺ salvage pathway: nicotinamide + PRPP → nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) + PPi . NMN is then converted to NAD⁺. NAMPT is a class II phosphoribosyltransferase (related to the NAPRTase family) . It exists as a homodimer and is inducible by stress, hypoxia, and cytokines, reflecting its role in metabolism and aging. NAMPT is widely expressed (e.g. adipose, liver) . Importantly, extracellular NAMPT (eNAMPT) has cytokine-like functions in immunity. Inhibitors of NAMPT (e.g. FK866) deplete NAD⁺ and are under investigation as anti-cancer agents. No inherited NAMPT deficiency in humans is reported; loss of NAMPT is embryonic lethal in mice.
11:33 PM
NOS (Nitric Oxide Synthases: eNOS, iNOS, nNOS) NOS enzymes catalyze the oxidative conversion of L-arginine to nitric oxide (NO) and L-citrulline, a key signaling pathway. They are NADPH- and tetrahydrobiopterin-dependent oxygenases. Three mammalian NOS isoforms exist: neuronal (nNOS/NOS1), inducible (iNOS/NOS2), and endothelial (eNOS/NOS3). Each forms a homodimer with an N-terminal oxygenase domain (binding heme, BH₄) and a C-terminal reductase domain (binding FAD/NADPH). Upon calcium/calmodulin activation (or cytokines for iNOS), NOS produces NO, a vasodilator and neurotransmitter. eNOS (endothelium) and nNOS (neurons) are constitutive; iNOS is induced in macrophages/inflammation. Dysregulated NOS activity is implicated in hypertension, septic shock, and neurotoxicity. NOS enzymes are targets of selective inhibitors (L-NAME inhibits all NOS; 7-NI is nNOS-selective) and modulators of their cofactor availability (e.g. BH₄ depletion uncouples NOS).

PDH (Pyruvate Dehydrogenase Complex) The PDH complex links glycolysis to the TCA cycle by irreversibly converting pyruvate + CoA + NAD⁺ → acetyl-CoA + CO₂ + NADH . It is a large mitochondrial complex of three enzyme components: E1 (pyruvate dehydrogenase, α and β subunits, including PDHA1), E2 (dihydrolipoamide acetyltransferase), and E3 (dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase). The E1 α1 subunit (PDHA1) carries the active site . Regulation occurs via phosphorylation by PDH kinases (inhibitory) and dephosphorylation by PDH phosphatases. Inhibited PDH diverts pyruvate to lactate (anaerobic conditions) or gluconeogenesis (in liver). Mutations in PDHA1 or other subunits cause PDH deficiency (neurological disorder with lactic acidosis) . PDH activity is tightly regulated by energy status (ADP/ATP, NADH/NAD⁺) and by acetyl-CoA levels. PEPCK (Phosphoenolpyruvate Carboxykinase) PEPCK catalyzes the conversion of oxaloacetate (OAA) to phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) + CO₂ in gluconeogenesis. In humans, two isoforms exist: cytosolic PCK1 (PEPCK-C) and mitochondrial PCK2 (PEPCK-M). The reaction consumes GTP: OAA + GTP → PEP + GDP + CO₂ . PCK1 (cytosolic, liver/kidney-enriched) is a rate-controlling step of gluconeogenesis and glyceroneogenesis. Its expression is induced by glucagon and cortisol and repressed by insulin . Mutations in PCK1 cause hereditary PEPCK deficiency (hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis). PEPCK activity is also post-translationally regulated by acetylation and substrate flux. In addition to gluconeogenesis, PEPCK supplies PEP for biosynthetic pathways (e.g. serine synthesis in cancer cells).

PFK (Phosphofructokinase-1) PFK-1 is the key regulatory enzyme of glycolysis. In humans, three tissue-specific PFK genes encode subunits (muscle PFKM, liver PFKL, platelet PFKP) . Active PFK is a tetramer composed of these subunits. It catalyzes fructose-6-phosphate + ATP → fructose-1,6-bisphosphate + ADP , committing glucose to glycolysis. PFK isoform expression varies by tissue (e.g. muscle has PFKM homo- or heterotetramers). Cancer cells often upregulate PFK to sustain aerobic glycolysis. PKM (Pyruvate Kinase M1/M2) PKM (encoded by PKM) produces pyruvate and ATP from PEP. Alternative splicing yields two isoforms: PKM1 (constitutively active, in muscle/brain) and PKM2 (regulatable, in proliferating tissues and cancers). The reaction is phosphoenolpyruvate + ADP → pyruvate + ATP . PKM2 activity is allosterically controlled by fructose-1,6-bisphosphate (activator) and by post-translational modifications (phosphorylation, acetylation). PKM1 is high-activity, driving glycolysis to completion. PKM2, by contrast, can exist in a less active dimeric form, diverting glycolytic intermediates to biosynthesis in tumors (Warburg effect). PKM is regulated transcriptionally by thyroid hormone (it binds thyroid hormone receptors ).

PNPO (Pyridoxine 5′-Phosphate Oxidase) PNPO catalyzes the final step in vitamin B₆ (pyridoxal phosphate, PLP) biosynthesis. It oxidizes pyridoxine 5′-phosphate (or pyridoxamine 5′-phosphate) to PLP using FMN and O₂ . PLP is a vital cofactor for aminotransferases and decarboxylases. Human PNPO is encoded by PNPO and is ubiquitously expressed (highest in liver, kidney) . PNPO activity is rate-limiting in PLP production, making dietary B6 availability critical. Mutations in PNPO cause neonatal epileptic encephalopathy (PNPO deficiency) due to low PLP . Treatment involves high-dose PLP. PNPO can be inhibited by substrate analogs; clinically, deficiency is often confused with pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy (ALDH7A1 mutations). PRODH (Proline Dehydrogenase/Proline Oxidase) PRODH (encoded by PRODH) is a mitochondrial FAD-dependent oxidase that catalyzes the first step of proline catabolism: L-proline + FAD → Δ¹-pyrroline-5-carboxylate + FADH₂. Inhibitors of PRODH are under study to modulate redox signaling in cancer cells.

Vagus Nerve as Modulator of the Brain–Gut Axis in Psychiatric and Inflammatory Disorders

‍ Authors: Breit S, Kupferberg A, et al Affiliations: University Hospital of Psychiatry, University of Bern; University Hospital Zurich Publication: Frontiers in Psychiatry Publication Date: March 13, 2018 URL: https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyt.2018.00044

Key Points

Bidirectional Highway: The vagus nerve links brain ↔ gut, with ~90 % sensory (afferent) and ~10 % motor (efferent) fibers. Therapeutic VNS: Electrical vagus-nerve stimulation is FDA-approved for epilepsy and shows promise for treatment-resistant depression, PTSD, and IBD. ️ Cholinergic Shield: Vagal ACh acting on α7-nicotinic receptors suppresses pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6), forming the “inflammatory reflex.” Second Brain: The enteric nervous system houses 100–500 million neurons—more than the spinal cord—and generates 95 % of body serotonin. Monoamine Modulator: VNS boosts brain serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine and encourages hippocampal neurogenesis, aiding mood regulation. Non-invasive Boosters: Slow breathing, meditation, yoga, and auricular tVNS raise vagal tone and cut anxiety/depression symptoms. ️ Appetite Signals: Gut hormones CCK (satiety), ghrelin (hunger), and leptin (energy balance) act via vagal afferents to fine-tune feeding and metabolism. Microbiome Crosstalk: Psychobiotic strains (e.g., L. rhamnosus, B. longum) alter behavior through vagal pathways—effects vanish after vagotomy. Anti-inflammatory Reflex: VNS lowers systemic inflammation in colitis, rheumatoid arthritis, and endotoxemia models, improving clinical markers. VNS Depression Relief: Chronic stimulation yields ~50 % acute response and lasting remission in treatment-resistant patients by boosting serotonin, norepinephrine, dopamine, and dampening inflammation. PTSD Extinction Aid: Pairing VNS with exposure therapy accelerates fear-extinction learning by enhancing mPFC–amygdala plasticity. Gut-Brain Nutrition: Probiotics, tailored diets, and antioxidants may complement VNS, targeting vagal immune and mood circuits—human data still preliminary. Research Gaps: Rigorous randomized trials are needed to define optimal VNS protocols, validate psychobiotics, and refine integrative brain-gut therapies. (edited)

Heptadecanoic acid (C17:0)

Odd-chain identity & sources: C17:0 is a 17-carbon saturated fatty acid found mainly in ruminant dairy fat (butter, milk), with smaller amounts in certain fish and rye, and can be elongated from C15:0 endogenously. Unique metabolism: Uses propionate-based β-oxidation and modest PPAR-δ activation to enhance mitochondrial biogenesis and metabolic flexibility. Metabolic health: Clinical and epidemiological data link C17:0 to improved insulin sensitivity, lower triglycerides, and reduced metabolic-syndrome markers. ❤️ Cardiovascular protection: Improves lipid ratios, supports endothelial nitric-oxide function, dampens CRP/IL-6, and is inversely associated with coronary heart-disease risk. Neuro support: Increases neuronal membrane fluidity, lessens microglial inflammation, and shows correlations with lower Alzheimer’s and mild-cognitive-impairment biomarkers. ️ Anti-cancer actions: Triggers caspase-driven apoptosis and curbs proliferation in gefitinib-resistant lung-cancer cells, hinting at adjuvant potential. Broad anti-inflammatory: Suppresses NF-κB and pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β), with observational links to lower autoimmune-disease incidence. Liver health: Mitigates hepatic steatosis, oxidative stress, and iron overload, pointing to protection against NAFLD progression. Dosing & kinetics: Study doses cluster around 50–500 mg / day for 8–12 weeks; lipophilic absorption peaks at 2–4 h, with a 24–48 h half-life. ️ Safety profile: Generally well-tolerated; occasional mild GI upset reported, but long-term human data and lipid-panel monitoring are still needed. Key synergies: Works with C15:0, omega-3 fats, CoQ10, polyphenols, and phospholipids for amplified PPAR signaling, anti-inflammation, and mitochondrial benefits. Research gaps: Optimal dosing, bioavailability tech, and high-quality RCTs are limited; natural whole-fat dairy may outperform isolated supplements pending further study.

AF710B (ANAVEX 3-71)

Dual-action agonist targeting M1 muscarinic & σ1 receptors delivers a novel cholinergic-sigma mechanism of action. Promising disease-modifier for Alzheimer’s, frontotemporal dementia & schizophrenia, tackling both symptoms and progression. Ultra-potent (μg/kg in rodents) with >50 000× safety margin versus effective dose. Restores cognition, memory & executive function with effects lasting ≥72 h post-dose. Lowers Aβ plaques and tau hyperphosphorylation via BACE1 inhibition, GSK3β inactivation & CDK5/p25 control. Dampens neuroinflammation, rescues synapses, and normalizes ER-mitochondrial calcium signaling for holistic neuroprotection. Improves all schizophrenia symptom domains without extrapyramidal side effects or cognitive dulling. Oral, CNS-penetrant small molecule shows linear, food- & gender-independent pharmacokinetics. ✅ Phase 1 trials found 5-200 mg daily well-tolerated with no serious adverse events or lab abnormalities. Holds FDA orphan-drug status for FTD; larger efficacy trials are needed to confirm optimal dosing & durability. Pitolisant

Pitolisant (Wakix) is a novel histamine H3 receptor antagonist and inverse agonist that represents a breakthrough in non-stimulant wake-promoting therapy. Unlike traditional stimulants, it works through the histaminergic system to enhance wakefulness, cognition, and neurological function while maintaining a favorable safety profile with minimal abuse potential.

TL;DR

Histaminergic mechanism – selective H3 antagonist & inverse agonist boosts brain histamine to promote wakefulness without dopaminergic stimulation. Regulatory status – first-in-class, non-controlled drug FDA-approved for excessive daytime sleepiness & cataplexy in narcolepsy. Sleep benefits – cuts daytime sleepiness 40-60 % and cataplexy 75-85 % while preserving normal nighttime REM / slow-wave architecture. Cognitive upsides – enhances attention, working memory, executive function and shows promise for ADHD symptom relief. ️ Broader neuro benefits – exhibits neuroprotective, anticonvulsant & anti-inflammatory effects with exploratory data in epilepsy, schizophrenia, dementia. Pharmacokinetics – ~90 % oral bioavailability, 3-4 h Tmax, 20 h half-life enables convenient once-daily dosing. ️ Personalized dosing – CYP2D6 poor metabolizers & hepatic or severe renal impairment need ~50 % dose cuts; watch CYP3A4 interactions & QTc. Safety profile – low abuse liability; most adverse events mild (headache, insomnia, nausea) and manageable with morning dosing. Formulations – immediate-release 4.45 mg & 17.8 mg tablets now; oral suspension, buccal/sublingual and IV research forms in pipeline. Synergies – complements sodium oxybate, good sleep hygiene, cognitive therapy, antioxidants/exercise for multimodal narcolepsy or cognitive care. Vs. stimulants – comparable wake promotion to modafinil/solriamfetol but with lower cardiovascular risk & distinct mechanism. Irdabisant contrast – higher-affinity H3 antagonist (Ki ≈ 2 nM) that failed in early trials, highlighting pitolisant’s uniquely successful clinical journey. Future horizons – ongoing trials exploring ADHD, Alzheimer’s, schizophrenia, fatigue disorders broaden its therapeutic landscape. (edited)

Central nervous system effects of TAK-653, an investigational alpha-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazole receptor (AMPAR) positive allosteric modulator in healthy volunteers

Mechanism: TAK-653 is a first-in-class AMPA-receptor positive allosteric modulator targeting rapid antidepressant effects via glutamatergic signaling. ️ Study Design: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial in 24 healthy adults tested single oral doses of 0.5 mg and 6 mg versus placebo. Pharmacokinetics: Predictable, dose-proportional absorption with fast Tmax (1.25-5 h) and long half-life (~33-48 h), confirming brain penetration. Cognitive Effects: The 6 mg dose boosted saccadic peak velocity (+15 deg/s), smooth pursuit (+2.3 %), and adaptive tracking (+1.7 %), resembling mild psychostimulant profiles. Stroop Anomaly: The 0.5 mg dose unexpectedly slowed Stroop performance, a non-linear cognitive effect absent at 6 mg. ️ Differentiation: No changes in body sway, mood, or “feeling high,” setting TAK-653 apart from caffeine, dexamphetamine, and modafinil. Adverse Events: Mild somnolence and headache were most common; no dissociation, seizures, or vital-sign abnormalities occurred. Neurobiology: TAK-653 enhances cortical excitability, BDNF release, and mTOR signaling without overstimulation risk. NeuroCart Utility: The battery sensitively captured AMPA-PAM effects, supporting its role in future glutamatergic drug studies. ️ Limitations: Small sample, single-dose design, seizure-risk dose cap, and healthy-volunteer setting constrain generalizability. Clinical Outlook: Findings support advancing TAK-653 to depressed patient trials, promising rapid action with benign tolerability. Takeaway: TAK-653 yields stimulant-like neural benefits minus subjective highs, validating AMPA-PAMs as a novel antidepressant strategy. Via @Yana乘

Therapeutic apheresis: A promising method to remove microplastics?

Study delivers first evidence that double-filtration apheresis (INUSpheresis) can remove micro- & nanoplastics (MNPs) from human blood, identified via ATR-FT-IR. 21 ME/CFS patients underwent ≥ 2 cycles; eluates held 14 MNP-like substances absent in filter prerinses, proving patient origin. Predominant particles matched nylon 6 (67.5 %) & polyurethane (35.3 %), with electrospun fibers < 100 nm enabling bloodstream entry. Up to 70 % of treated patients reported significant symptom relief, mirroring earlier ME/CFS & long-COVID apheresis outcomes. Results bolster the hypothesis that circulating MNPs drive multisystem disorders—cardio-metabolic, neurocognitive, endocrine, reproductive & oncologic. ️ Device’s ≤ 200 nm double-filter shows existing clinical tech can feasibly clear nanoscale plastics. Analysis was qualitative only; quantitative pyrolysis-GC-MS & pre/post plasma assays are needed to gauge removal efficiency. ️ Rigorous contamination controls (filter prerinses, strict sampling) confirm detected particles weren’t lab artifacts. Rising airborne particles ≤ 10 µm align with ME/CFS incidence, positioning apheresis as a potential exposure-mitigation therapy. Study shifts the narrative from prevention-only to active detoxification options for ubiquitous microplastic pollution. Future research must optimize filter design, enlarge cohorts, correlate particle clearance with clinical gains & pair treatment with preventive strategies. Despite limitations, this May 2025 Brevia in Brain Medicine seeds a paradigm change in environmental health management.

Pre-resolving mediators are specialized lipid compounds derived from omega-3s (DHA/EPA) like 17-HDHA, 14-HDHA, and 18-HEPE that kickstart active resolution of inflammation They act as intermediate metabolites in lipoxygenase pathways, balancing pro- and anti-inflammatory signals and preventing chronic inflammation by promoting tissue homeostasis ️ Key benefits include stopping neutrophil infiltration, enhancing macrophage efferocytosis (MerTK, CD36), debris clearance, and supporting lymphatic drainage for repair In cardiovascular health, they improve endothelial function (eNOS/NO), stabilize plaques, enhance angiogenesis via VEGF, reduce post-MI scarring, and lower blood pressure Neuroprotection is mediated through upregulation of BDNF/CREB, improved synaptic plasticity (NMDA/AMPA), reduced microglial inflammation, autophagy induction, and mitochondrial protection Immune modulation involves boosting pathogen clearance, balancing T-cell responses (Tregs vs. Th17), enhancing antigen presentation, and preventing autoimmune activation Metabolic benefits feature improved insulin sensitivity (GLUT4), increased mitochondrial biogenesis (PGC-1α), reduced hepatic steatosis (PPAR-α), adipose browning (UCP1), and better β-cell function They target genes like ALOX15, PTGS2, NF-κB, PPARA/PPARG, BDNF, VEGFA, SIRT1, and autophagy genes (ATG5/7, LC3) to orchestrate resolution and repair Available in diverse forms: fish-oil concentrates, algae-derived precursors, synthetic isolates (17-HDHA, 14-HDHA, 18-HEPE), liposomal and injectable formulations Typical dosages range from 1–3 g EPA/DHA daily or 25–200 mg isolated mediators, with bioavailability enhanced by liposomal or phospholipid delivery; 4–12 weeks for full effects Side effects are generally mild (GI upset, fishy aftertaste) but include bleeding risk with anticoagulants and rare allergic reactions or transient fatigue ️ Caveats include limited long-term safety data, genetic variability affecting efficacy, high costs for synthetic forms, and necessity for medical supervision in certain populations Synergistic partners like olive-oil polyphenols, curcumin, resveratrol, quercetin, magnesium, vitamin D, probiotics, and sulforaphane enhance stability and therapeutic effects Compared to downstream resolvins/protectins/maresins, pre-resolving mediators have longer half-lives but require enzymatic conversion to active SPMs

Impact of intestinal disorders on central and peripheral nervous system diseases

Publication: Neurobiology of Disease Publication Date: January 13, 2022

Key Points

Gut-brain communication is bidirectional; intestinal disorders like IBS can send pathological signals to the brain—an angle still under-researched. IBS/IBD affect up to 23 % of people worldwide with a strong female bias, creating a huge global health and economic burden. Intestinal inflammation breaks tight-junctions, producing a “leaky gut” that lets microbes and toxins enter the bloodstream, driving chronic low-grade inflammation. Circulating cytokines weaken blood-brain barrier junctions, opening the door for peripheral immune cells and endotoxins to invade the CNS. Neuroinflammation that follows raises the odds of Alzheimer’s (6 ×), Parkinson’s (35 %), multiple sclerosis, depression, and anxiety. Dysbiosis—↑ Firmicutes:Bacteroidetes ratio, ↓ SCFA-producers—cuts protective butyrate and other metabolites that normally shore up gut & brain barriers. Enteric-nervous-system remodeling and altered vagus-nerve signaling provide neural highways that can magnify or buffer gut-derived brain effects. ‍⚕️ Sex hormones shape barrier function and stress reactivity, explaining female predominance in IBS, MS, AD, versus male predominance in PD. Lifespan patterns show early gut disease overlapping MS onset while later gut peaks track with AD/PD, highlighting age-specific intervention windows. Core cascade: leaky gut → systemic cytokines → BBB breach → immune-cell brain infiltration → neurodegeneration. Clinically, IBD patients need routine neuro-psych screening, and therapies that restore gut barrier & microbiome may forestall brain disorders. Future work must pin down gut-vs-brain timing, validate biomarkers, and test gut-targeted treatments in long-term trials.

Intranasal insulin enhances brain functional connectivity mediating the relationship between adiposity and subjective feeling of hunger

Publication: Scientific Reports Publication Date: 2017 DOI URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-01907-w

Key Points

Brain insulin sensitivity links metabolism, cognition, and the default-mode network, making it a pivotal therapeutic target. A single 160 U intranasal insulin dose bypasses peripheral circulation and reaches the brain within 30 minutes, enabling rapid action. Lean and overweight/obese young adults responded similarly, suggesting broad applicability across BMI ranges. Insulin strengthened functional connectivity between prefrontal DMN hubs and the right hippocampus—key for memory and self-control. ️ Greater dorsal medial PFC–hippocampus connectivity predicted lower hunger ratings two hours post-dose. The same connectivity increase correlated with visceral fat and mediated the VAT-to-hunger relationship, disrupting the “fat-hunger” feedback loop. ️ Mediation analysis confirmed hippocampal connectivity as the critical intermediary (standardized indirect effect = –0.34). Hypothalamic connectivity gains appeared only in insulin-sensitive participants, highlighting central-peripheral synergy. ️ Mechanistically, insulin enhances hippocampal plasticity and may suppress circulating FFAs, sharpening interoceptive satiety signals. Intranasal insulin shows promise for weight management and cognitive enhancement, with personalized benefits based on insulin sensitivity. Connectivity changes emerged within 30 minutes of dosing, underscoring insulin’s rapid neuromodulatory power. ❗ Limitations—student-only cohort, no cognitive testing, and potential systemic spillover—warrant larger, more diverse trials.

When adverse effects are seen as desirable: Abuse potential of the newer generation antiepileptic drugs

Publication: Epilepsy & Behavior Publication Date: 2017

Key Points

Newer-generation AEDs like pregabalin show unexpected abuse potential, driving tighter regulatory scrutiny and controlled-substance scheduling. UK prescriptions for gabapentinoids surged (pregabalin +300%, gabapentin +150%), paralleling rising diversion and deaths. Human abuse-potential studies use double-blind crossover designs in recreational users, measuring Drug-Liking VAS, ARCI MBG/PCAG, and Subjective Drug Value. Perampanel displays clear dose-dependent liking; supratherapeutic doses resemble alprazolam/ketamine effects, earning Schedule III status. ️ Eslicarbazepine shows minimal euphoria versus alprazolam across doses and remains unscheduled. Lacosamide at 800 mg matches alprazolam in euphoria and drug liking, leading to Schedule V classification. Brivaracetam demonstrates increased liking at 1000 mg yet less sedation than alprazolam, resulting in Schedule V placement. Scheduling decisions hinge on subjective liking and dose-response data, prioritizing public-health risk over therapeutic usage patterns. Study weaknesses—suboptimal dose selection and lax qualification thresholds—can skew abuse-liability estimates. Postmarketing surveillance reveals real-world abuse, diversion, and mortality signals often missed during clinical trials. ‍⚕️ Clinicians must balance seizure control with vigilant monitoring for aberrant drug-seeking, especially in at-risk patients. Diverse mechanisms (AMPA antagonism, SV2A binding, sodium-channel modulation) don’t guarantee low abuse risk—dose and context remain pivotal.

Magnesium-L-threonate alleviate colonic inflammation and memory impairment in chronic-plus-binge alcohol feeding mice

Chronic-plus-binge alcohol mice given MgT (Magnesium L-Threonate, 100 – 200 mg/kg) showed systemic inflammation, gut leakage, and memory loss reversed versus alcohol-only controls. ️ MgT cut blood, colon, and brain TNF-α / IL-1β by ~30-50 %, taming systemic and neuro-inflammation. Antioxidant defenses surged—SOD & GSH-Px up 40-60 %—while oxidative-stress marker 4-HNE plummeted. Tight-junction proteins ZO-1 & Claudin-1 rebounded, sealing the intestinal barrier and preventing endotoxin spill-over. Gut microbiota shifted toward beneficial Akkermansia, Blautia & Odoribacter while curbing Alloprevotella, Clostridium & Ruminococcus. Alpha & beta diversity rose, and PICRUSt2 predicted boosts in amino-acid metabolism, tryptophan synthesis & oxidative phosphorylation. Hippocampal integrity and serotonin/NMDAR signaling recovered, cutting escape latency and raising platform crossings in the Morris water maze. Positive correlations linked Mg²⁺ and 5-HT with antioxidant enzymes & barrier proteins, while harmful cytokines aligned with deleterious microbes. Threonate enabled brain-penetrant magnesium; neither ion nor ligand alone improved cognition, proving essential synergy. Higher dose (200 mg/kg) consistently outperformed 100 mg/kg with no adverse events, showing clear dose-response and safety. Findings position MgT as a practical dietary supplement to prevent alcohol-related colitis, dysbiosis, and cognitive decline. Overall, MgT delivers a multi-target gut-brain axis rescue—antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, barrier-repair, and microbiota-modulation—reversing alcohol damage.

Modulation of Amyloid and Tau Aggregation to Alleviate Cognitive Impairment in a Transgenic Mouse Model of Alzheimer’s Disease
Thus, we report a small molecule drug candidate, DN5355, with a dual-targeting function toward aggregates of both Aβ and tau. DN5355 was selected through a series of four screenings assessing 52 chemicals for their functions to inhibit and reverse the aggregation of Aβ and tau by utilizing thioflavin T. When orally administered to AD transgenic mouse model 5XFAD, DN5355 significantly reduced cerebral Aβ plaques and hyperphosphorylated tau tangles. In Y-maze spontaneous alteration and contextual fear conditioning tests, 5XFAD mice showed amelioration of cognitive deficits upon the oral administration of DN5355.

mechanism elucidated by @Takistron A PAM of the α1A-Adrenergic receptor rescues biomarker, long-term potentiation, and cognitive deficits in Alzheimer’s disease mouse models without effects on blood pressure
In this report, we now demonstrate the in vivo characteristics of Compound 3 (Cmpd-3) in two genetically-different Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) mouse models. Drug metabolism and pharmacokinetic studies indicate sufficient brain penetrance and rapid uptake into the brain with low to moderate clearance, and a favorable inhibition profile against the major cytochrome p450 enzymes. Oral administration of Cmpd-3 (3–9 mg/kg QD) can fully rescue long-term potentiation defects and AD biomarker profile (amyloid β-40, 42) within 3 months of dosing to levels that were non-significant from WT controls and which outperformed donepezil (1 mg/kg QD). Long-term and high-dose in vivo studies with Cmpd-3 revealed no effects on blood pressure. Our results suggest that Cmpd-3 can maintain lasting therapeutic levels and efficacy with disease modifying effects with a once per day dosing regimen in AD mouse models with no observed side effects.

The first selected compound is 3-(aminoethyl)1-methylindol-5-ol (MetI, Figure 2, upper panel). Compared with serotonin, this compound has a methyl substitution at the amine of the indol group, which, in principle, would diminish the capacity for hydrogen bonding with residue S5.46 in helix 5, but would still allow interaction with N6.55, therefore promoting AA over IP signaling. The second candidate, 5-methyltryptamine (MetT, Figure 2, upper panel), has a methyl substitution in the position occupied by the hydroxyl group in serotonin. According to our hypothesis, this compound should show a decreased ability to form a hydrogen bond with residue N6.55 hence making it a biased agonist by promoting IP over AA signaling. Preprint Exploring a Druggable Hydrophobic Tunnel in the 5-HT2A Receptor with Potent Phenethylamines
The experimental 5-HT2AR structures have identified a hydrophobic tunnel lateral to the orthosteric site, situated in between the transmembrane helices 4 and 5. Molecular modeling, structure-activity relationship determination, and mutagenesis experiments demonstrate that the agonist potencies at the 5-HT2AR exhibited by analogs with 4-substituents with at least four heavy atoms are rooted in their ability to protrude into and form interactions within this tunnel. Thus, these findings provide new insights into the molecular basis for phenethylamine-induced 5-HT2AR activation and identify this tunnel, for the first time, as a druggable region to employ in designing potent 5-HT2AR agonists.

Effects of a Serotonergic Psychedelic on the Lipid Bilayer
Also, the psychoplastogenic effects of these molecules correlate with their lipophilicity, leading to suggestions that they act by influencing the intracellular receptors. However, their lipophilicity also implies that a significant quantity of lipids is accumulated in the lipid bilayer, potentially altering the physical properties of the membrane. Solid-state NMR spectroscopy shows that the DOI strongly induces disorder in the lipid acyl chains. Atomic force microscopy shows that it can shrink the ordered domains in a biphasic lipid bilayer and can reduce the force needed to form nanopores in the membrane. Fluorescence correlation spectroscopy shows that DOI can promote vesicle association, and total internal fluorescence microscopy shows that it enhances vesicle fusion to a supported lipid bilayer. While serotonin has also recently been shown to cause similar effects, DOI is more than two orders of magnitude more potent in evoking these.

We describe the synthesis and characterization of three U50,488 analogues, 1, 2, and 3. Compound 3 showed no significant side effects on any test. Signaling bias did not correlate with the antinociceptive or side effects of any compounds and knockout of β-arrestin2 had no effect on U50,488-induced sedation or motor incoordination.
